implementation_notes: Kotlin adds nothing authorization-specific, so the idiomatic mapping is a fun interface Policy { fun decide(ctx: SecurityContext, action: Action, resource: Resource): Decision } - SAM conversion lets rules be written as lambdas - plus a small guard function or framework interceptor that calls the policy and throws a dedicated AccessDeniedException on denial. What replaces the classic structure: a single-method fun interface plus an extension or top-level guard function replaces the abstract Policy/Guard class pair, and Kotlin's non-null types keep a missing security context out of the guard signature. The fuller OO structure is still justified when several policy families share configuration or rule state (for example a rule engine loaded from a file).
idiom_name: fun interface Policy + guard function (SAM rules)
pitfalls: require()/check() throw IllegalArgumentException/IllegalStateException, which frameworks map to 400/500 rather than 403; throw a dedicated access-denied exception the error handler understands.
A SAM-converted lambda allocated per request defeats the point of a Policy value; keep one policy instance as a top-level val or inject it.
Non-null signatures only help if the security context really is non-null at the boundary; a context built from unverified headers should be rejected, not wrapped in a default object.
